sources.note: 2024 exhibition account checked directly: varied regional peoples, Late Bronze Age background, Persian intervention 513 BCE and Roman province around 46 CE. No claim of a unified Bronze Age kingdom.

sources.title: National Archaeological Institute with Museum: the Valchitran treasure
sources.note: Bulgarian institutional account, 2012, checked directly: discovery 1924, 13 surviving objects, 12.425 kg, manufacturing and debated function. Uses late fourteenth/early thirteenth century BCE dating; newer museum Vault overview more broadly assigns transition from Late Bronze to Early Iron Age. Public date therefore broad Late Bronze Age, not an exact year. Pig-feeding anecdote and confident Dionysos dedication omitted.

sources.title: Charles University: excavations at Pistiros
sources.note: Excavator Jan Bouzek account checked directly: houses, pottery, metallurgy, coin hoard, astragals, possible tavern. Adzhiyska Vodenitsa identification as Pistiros remains debated; 2026 study still uses it. No claim that three astragals establish exact modern game rules.

sources.title: Emil Nankov: mobile cooking supports from Emporion Pistiros, 2026
sources.note: Primary research abstract checked directly; DOI 10.57573/be-ja.16.57-79. Ceramic objects reinterpreted from bellows nozzles to cooking supports; early fourth-century BCE sunken homes and domestic waste contexts. Distinguish kitchen objects from genuine other metallurgical finds.

sources.title: PHI Greek Inscriptions: SEG 43:486, Pistiros charter
sources.note: Exact scholarly Greek transcription directly checked. Heading after 359 BCE; line 8 unbracketed τοῖς ἐμπορίταις means to the merchants. Accents and lower-case presentation editorial, not a facsimile. Greek regional witness, not the Thracian language.

sources.title: Denise Demetriou: Pistiros and a North Aegean Trade Network, 2010
sources.note: Primary scholarly article opening printed p77 checked directly: merchant rights, regional dynasts, after Kotys death 359 BCE; stone reused and location disputed. Author advocates coastal location against majority inland identification, so public passage acknowledges debate.

sources.title: UNESCO: Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak
sources.note: Direct official description: discovered 1944, late fourth century BCE, corridor and round chamber painted with funeral scenes, near Seuthopolis. Images of elite rites not evidence for every family household.

sources.title: UNESCO: Thracian Tomb of Sveshtari
sources.note: Direct official description and significance: third century BCE, 1982 discovery, ten female/plant figures, surviving polychromy including blue/red/lilac. Getic monument, not a generic temple.
